newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korea has high-level power shift.
newsitem.headline: North Korea has high-level power shift.

text.p: North Korea on Friday announced the appointment of an acting premier to replace Kang Song-san, the sixth-ranked official in its power structure.

The announcement added to speculation about turmoil in North Korea's leadership since the defection in Beijing on February 12 of Hwang Jang-yop, a close advisor to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, and its 24th-ranked official.
A report on Pyongyang Radio said Deputy Prime Minister Premier Hong Song-nam had been appointed acting premier.

The report, monitored by the Tokyo-based news agency Radiopress, which follows North Korea's media, gave no reason why Hong, 73, was taking over the post of premier which Kang, 66, had held since December 1992.
But Radiopress analyst Noriyuki Suzuki said Kang had not been seen in public since January 1996 and speculated the health of the long-time diabetes sufferer had deteriorated.
In Seoul, a senior official of the National Unification Ministry also said Kang had not appeared in public for a year because of illness.
Other analysts said the timing could be a clue to other factors.

"I believe the change has something to do with Kang's health, but the question is why is the appointment being announced now," said Masao Okonogi, professor of Korean History at Tokyo's Keio University.
"We can't rule out other possibilities, such as a leadership purge connected with Hwang's defection," he told Reuters.
Suzuki said Kang ranked sixth in North Korea's power structure while Hong, a vice premier since October 1987 and a Politburo alternate member since March 1989, ranked 19th.

Kang, like the defector Hwang, was a supporter of opening up the Stalinist nation to economic reform to save it from collapse after two years of devastating floods which have set off a widespread famine.
Talks on the fate of Hwang have been put on hold by the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Hwang arrived at Seoul's consular office in Beijing with an aide on February 12, forcing China to tread a fine line between ideological ally North Korea and new business partner South Korea.
Suzuki said Hong, expected to be confirmed as permanent premier once North Korea's parliament convenes after a three-year recess, has close ties with the Chinese leadership.
In May 1996 he led a North Korean delegation to Beijing where he met Chinese prime minister Li Peng and won a pledge of 20,000 tonnes of badly needed food aid.
Born in 1924, Hong graduated from Pyongyang's elite Kim Il-sung University and studied machinery engineering in Czechoslovakia.
In his political life, he has held mainly economic posts, including chairman of the State Planning Commission.
